name: PT IMC Pelita Logistik Tbk

frontmatter.title: IMC Pelita Logistik - net cash cannot fix a sub-cost-of-capital fleet
frontmatter.summary: IMC Pelita Logistik moves coal and dry bulk on owned tugs, barges and floating loading facilities. The downcycle is real, the balance sheet is net cash, and the stock trades below book. But the fleet earns a low return on capital even after our margin recovery, the final shipping levy and a full replacement-capex charge cut free cash flow, and the market already discounts a much faster recovery than we forecast. We move to REDUCE.
thesis: PSSI is a shipping operator, not a coal trader or a miner: it is paid to move tonnes, so the economic drivers are fleet utilisation and tariffs, not the price of the cargo it carries [S2].

The downcycle is real but it was a volume cycle, not a tariff collapse: volume fell from 21.0 Mt in FY2024 to 14.0 Mt in FY2025 while revenue per tonne rose, and nine-month 2026 revenue of US$35.1m was below the US$44.5m earned a year earlier [S2, S3, F1, F2].

The balance sheet is the floor: at September 2026 the company held US$56.4m of cash and deposits and US$7.5m of financial assets against US$14.2m of bank loans, and the fleet's net book value was US$80.1m [S3].
The floor is not the value: book equity of US$150.2m earns a forecast ROE of 2.0% by FY2030E, and the DCF at a full replacement-capex charge gives Rp271 against the Rp336 price [S0, S3].
The weighted target is Rp267, -20.6% below the last close; the market price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 13.5% against the 5.0% we forecast [S0].

catalysts.event: Cum date for the treasury-share bonus; distribution on 27 November 2026
2027 RKAB quota approval, the main swing factor for customer coal volumes and barge demand
FY2026 audited results; watch the full-year gross margin against the nine-month run-rate and the capex peak
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision under the stated payout policy
Staged delivery of the six renewal vessels and first disclosure of their utilisation

blocks.text: **Rating REDUCE · target Rp267 · last close Rp336 · return -20.6%**

This revision fixes the share and price basis, and changes the valuation, not the business description. Every per-share figure is now struck on one share count: the 5,161m shares outstanding on the 19 October 2026 distribution base, which is the count the cum-bonus Rp336 close is quoted on. The one-for-thirty treasury bonus lifts that to a larger post-bonus count after the 6 November 2026 ex-date, but because the distribution is a pro-rata transfer of existing shares the economics per unit of ownership are unchanged: the same target that reads Rp267 on the cum-bonus base reads lower per post-bonus share, and the return of -20.6% is the same on either basis [S0, S7, F38, F41]. We have dropped the P/BV cross-check because the own-history book multiple was struck when ROE was near its cycle peak, charged the final shipping levy through operating costs, lifted long-run capex to the depreciation charge, and restated the balance sheet to 30 September 2026. The cumulative effect is a lower target and a change of rating to REDUCE [S0, S3, S7, F38, F40].

The company is still in the trough of its cycle. Revenue fell from US$102.4m in FY2023 to US$57.1m in FY2025, and the nine months to September 2026 produced US$35.1m against US$44.5m a year earlier [S0, S3]. The decline was volume-led: cargo volume fell from 21.0 Mt to 14.0 Mt, while revenue per tonne rose, so the earlier statement that volumes and tariffs both fell was wrong and is corrected here [S2, F1, F2]. The FY2025 net profit was US$0.2m, down from US$14.2m, and the first nine months of 2026 produced a net loss of US$0.8m [S0, S3].

The variant view is not that the cycle is about to boom; it is that the market is already paying for a faster recovery than the fleet's economics support. At the cum-bonus Rp336 close the equity is worth IDR1.73tn, and cash, deposits and financial assets net of bank loans are more than half of that market value, while cash, funds and the fleet's net book value together exceed it; the asset backing is the real support [S3, S0, F56]. But the operating business earns a low return on that capital: the DCF gives Rp271 a share, and the market-implied FY2027E revenue growth of 13.5% is far above our 5.0% [S0]. The asset backing limits how far the shares should fall, not whether they are too high today.

What moves the value, in order: the tariff and utilisation recovery as the oversupplied barge market absorbs capacity; the fleet-renewal programme and whether the new barges earn a return above their cost; and the pace at which the large net cash position is returned to shareholders or reinvested [S2, S5]. The dividend is small at the trough, and the stated policy caps distribution at a share of net profit, so the cash is not automatically a shareholder return [S2].

Coal barge operators sit between the mine and the export terminal or power plant. They load at a jetty or transshipment anchorage, carry the cargo downriver or along the coast, and transfer it to a mother vessel or unload it at a port. The business is asset-heavy and operationally geared: a barge earns money only when it is moving, so utilisation and the freight rate per tonne matter far more than the coal price itself. In a tight fleet market tariffs rise and older tonnage is sold at a gain; in an oversupplied market tariffs fall faster than costs, and the operator absorbs the difference. The balance sheet, the age profile of the fleet and the contract book are therefore the things to watch through a cycle.

PT IMC Pelita Logistik Tbk was founded in 2007, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2017 and changed its name from PT Pelita Samudera Shipping Tbk in February 2023 [S2]. It describes itself as a maritime shipping and integrated logistics company providing transshipment, inter-island and international dry-bulk transportation, with a primary focus on the coal mining supply chain [S2]. Its fleet at the end of FY2024 numbered 52 vessels and at the end of FY2025 48, as older tonnage was sold; it operated 47 vessels at September 2026 before the new-build programme [S2, S5, F8, F28, F53].

The revenue mix is a shipping mix. In FY2025 floating loading and freight earned US$38.0m, time charter earned US$16.9m, the bunker adjustment added US$1.2m, and demurrage, warehouse rental and other services made up the remainder, for total revenue of US$57.1m [S2]. The company runs a deliberate balance between medium-term time-charter and freight-charter contracts and selective spot work, which management says gives revenue visibility while preserving flexibility [S2]. It does not disclose contract lengths, day rates or a backlog, so the visibility is asserted rather than quantified; we treat the contract book as real but thin evidence.

Customers are coal miners, shippers and industrial buyers. The notes single out only one customer above the disclosure threshold, PT Samudera Nusa Perkasa, at US$5.7m of sales in FY2025, which is a low concentration for an Indonesian coal-logistics name and a genuine positive [S2]. The customer names behind the rest of the book are not disclosed. The company does not name its largest customers, so we cannot test renewal risk customer by customer; the annual report's claim of long-term relationships is the only evidence [S2].

Strategy as management frames it has several parts: keep fleet utilisation high through route and schedule adjustments; strengthen the contract portfolio by balancing time charter and spot; and develop an integrated logistics platform through warehouse assets and the OLI, OKI and PSP entities in Karawang [S2]. The integrated-logistics initiative is early stage, with limited contribution to date, and the company says so [S2]. The more material capital decision is the fleet renewal: new tugs and barges have been ordered at Batam yards, with each new barge carrying more than 10,000 tonnes, and delivery staged according to market conditions [S5]. Management frames it as reliability and flexibility for customers rather than as capacity growth, which is consistent with a replacement programme in an oversupplied market [S5].

Control is concentrated. PT Indoprima Marine held 43.8% of the issued shares at the end of FY2025, and PT Himpunan Primajaya is the controlling party of Indoprima Marine and the ultimate controlling shareholder [S2]. The public free float is 16.2%, thin enough that the house applies a liquidity discount to the valuation [S0]. The company is distributing 172.0m treasury shares as a bonus at a ratio of one new share for every 30 held; because the shares come from treasury and the distribution is pro rata, total issued shares are unchanged and no holder's percentage changes. The press reports of the controlling and public stakes rising are an arithmetic error from applying the bonus ratio to the percentage rather than to the share count, and we do not repeat them [S6, S7, F27, F41]. The company employs 92 people directly, which is consistent with an outsourced-crew, asset-owning model [S0].

The group structure is a parent with operating subsidiaries for sea freight, property and the new logistics entities; the company reports no bonds, sukuk or convertible securities outstanding at the end of FY2025 [S2]. That simplicity is a governance positive: the capital structure is bank debt and leases, not layered securities with conversion or coupon risk.

The industry is Indonesian coal distribution and maritime logistics. The annual report frames it through the domestic market obligation: coal remained the main source of national power generation, domestic obligation supply reached a large share of national output, and most production was still exported, so the movement from mine to port and from port to buyer is a permanent need [S2]. The coal deck we carry prices the seaborne market, and its path runs from US$137/t in FY2026E to US$118/t in FY2027E and US$105/t in the long run, with spot at US$150/t [deck]. For a barge operator the absolute price matters less than the volume it implies and the tariff the fleet can charge; a lower coal price that keeps Indonesian volumes steady is not bad for PSSI, and a price spike that curtails customer production is not good. The deck is context for the revenue path rather than a mechanical driver: the corporate template takes revenue from our growth assumption, and we set that assumption against the deck's volume implication, not the other way round [S2, deck].

The direct commodity cost is fuel. Marine diesel and fuel oil cost US$12.2m in FY2025, a material share of cost of revenue of US$51.6m, and the oil deck's Brent path runs from US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E to US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E [S2, deck]. The company recovers most of a fuel move through tariff resets, but not all, so a sustained oil spike compresses the spread; the nine-month 2026 result shows the mechanism working in the other direction as fuel costs normalised [S3].

Regulation shapes the business in three ways. First, RKAB production quotas govern how much coal the customers can mine, and therefore how many tonnes they need moved; management explicitly cites RKAB uncertainty as a cause of the volume decline [S2]. Second, the domestic market obligation and the price cap on domestic-power coal affect where coal flows and which logistics routes are busy [S2]. Third, shipping income is taxed through a final levy on vessel-operation and charter revenue at a rate of 1.2%, plus corporate income tax on the residual; the levy is charged even when the pre-levy result is a loss, which is why the trough tax line is not zero and why we model it explicitly [S2, S3, F43, F52]. We do not model a royalty or a mining tax because the company has none [S2].

Competition is fragmented and the fleet is oversupplied. The annual report says fleet supply was relatively high in the market and that this affected freight rates and vessel utilisation, which is the clearest statement of the competitive problem [S2]. Barriers to entry are capital and contracts rather than geology: a new entrant can buy or charter barges, but it needs customer relationships, port access and a safety record. PSSI's position is that of a mid-sized, long-established operator with a mixed fleet and a diversified customer list, not the largest and not a price-setter. Its moat is the fleet's suitability for shallow-draft river and transshipment work, the switching cost of integrating a barge schedule into a mine's export chain, and a customer base that is less concentrated than the sector norm [S2].

The five forces are mixed. Buyer power is moderate: the disclosed customer concentration is low, but coal miners and traders are sophisticated and can re-tender, and the customer is larger than the operator in most cases [S2]. Supplier power is low: shipyards, crew, fuel and spare parts are available from many sources. New entrants are a real threat in an oversupplied market, because additional barges can be chartered in. Substitutes are the energy transition and the substitution of rail or truck haulage for short coastal moves, both slow within our horizon. Rivalry is high on price and utilisation, and the industry's returns depend on fleet discipline, which is exactly what the downcycle has tested.

The company's own fleet data show the operating leverage. Tug-and-barge utilisation was 94.0% in FY2025, while floating loading facilities ran lower and motor vessels lower still [S2]. A high utilisation rate on a falling revenue base means the tariff, not the idle time, did the damage; that is consistent with the company's account of oversupply and price pressure [S2]. The renewal programme is a bet that newer, larger barges will win the work that is available on better terms, and it is the single largest discretionary capital commitment in the forecast [S5].

The revenue history is a full cycle compressed into a few lines. Revenue fell from US$119.3m in FY2022 to US$102.4m, US$81.2m and US$57.1m, a cumulative decline driven first by the coal-price correction and then by volume pressure [S0, S2]. Volume fell from 21.0 Mt in FY2024 to 14.0 Mt in FY2025, while revenue per tonne rose as tariffs reset; that is the more accurate reading of the downcycle, and it matters because a volume-led trough can recover with coal output even if tariffs stay flat [S2, F1, F2, F30]. Gross margin moved from 36.3% to 36.8%, 26.1% and 9.6%, and EBITDA margin, restated for the true depreciation charge, moved from 31.5% to 21.3% [S0, S2]. Net profit to parent fell from US$42.2m to US$0.2m [S0].

The data pack materially understates depreciation, and we restate it. The pack shows a token FY2025 D&A charge, while the fixed-asset note of the audited accounts reports US$12.8m of fixed-asset depreciation charged to profit or loss, part in cost of revenue and part in operating expenses [S2]. FY2024 was US$15.0m [S2]. We use the filing's figures for both years, which lifts historical EBITDA from the pack's near-zero print to a positive number and changes every margin and multiple built on it; this is a restatement of wrong data, not a modelling choice [S2].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. In FY2025 cost of revenue of US$51.6m comprised depreciation, US$12.2m of fuel, US$8.3m of charter hire, and the remainder in spare parts, vessel operations, crew, repairs, port charges and insurance [S2]. Operating expenses were US$6.1m, including US$1.3m of directors' fees, which is a high charge for a company of this size and a governance point we return to in section six [S2]. Because a large share of the cost base is fixed in the short run, a fall in revenue hits gross profit disproportionately, and the FY2025 gross margin of 9.6% is the result [S2].

The nine months to September 2026 show the trough, but not a straight-line recovery. Revenue was US$35.1m against US$44.5m, gross profit was US$3.6m, and the net result was a loss of US$0.8m [S3]. The quarterly path is uneven: the first quarter was barely profitable at the gross line, the second quarter was the strongest of the three, and the third quarter eased back to below the nine-month average, so the earlier claim that the margin recovered from the first quarter and that this was the first sign of stabilisation skipped the second-quarter peak [S3]. We do not extrapolate a single quarter into a recovery, and we do not describe a sequential decline as stabilisation; the FY2026E forecast is set from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate [S3].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual at last year's economics and then lets the cycle recover modestly. FY2026E revenue is US$48.0m, a growth rate of -16.0% on the nine-month run-rate, with a gross margin of 10.4% and EBITDA of US$9.7m [S0, S3]. The FY2026E revenue is below FY2025 because the nine-month actual is below the prior year; the margin is close to the last actual once the final shipping levy, which we charge through operating costs, is added back, and the like-for-like comparison is disclosed in the operating-cost paragraph below [S2, S3]. Revenue then grows as the new vessels join the fleet, and the gross margin recovers to 19.0% by FY2030E, still below the 26.1% achieved in FY2024 and far below the FY2023 peak [S2]. The recovery is operating leverage on a partly fixed fleet cost base, not a return to the boom.

The recovery is deliberately not a flat-COGS assumption. Fuel and charter hire are variable with volume and together are a material share of cost of revenue, so a revenue path driven by new vessels carries incremental fuel and charter cost; we let roughly two-fifths of the cost base flex with volume, which produces the margin path above rather than holding absolute COGS flat while revenue grows [S2, F20, F21]. The earlier terminal margin was delivered by flat absolute COGS and is not supported by the evidence; the new path is lower but still well above the nine-month trough [S2, S3].

The final shipping levy is a real cash cost at the trough. The company pays a 1.2% final tax on vessel-operation and charter revenue, and the nine-month 2026 charge was US$0.3m even though the pre-final-tax result was a loss [S3, F43, F52]. Because the engine's free-cash-flow formula carries only a profit tax, we include the levy in operating costs, which is why the reported opex ratio rises to 11.7% and why forecast EBITDA is after the levy and not directly comparable with the pre-levy historical print [S3, F43]. Corporate income tax at the statutory rate then applies to the residual; the combined burden reconciles to the nine-month run-rate [S3, F52].

Capital expenditure is the swing factor in the near term. The company spent US$9.6m on fixed assets in FY2025 but US$15.6m in the nine months to September 2026 as the renewal programme was paid for [S2, S3]. We carry capex at 40.0% of revenue in FY2026E, falling to 20.0% in FY2027E and the FY2025 actual 17.0% through FY2030E while the renewed fleet is young; from FY2031E the long-run ratio rises to the depreciation charge of 21.5% [S2, S3, S5]. The earlier assumption held capex at 17.0% in perpetuity, which added roughly two-fifths of terminal free cash flow from under-investment; we do not keep that [S2, S3]. The consequence is a negative free cash flow year in FY2026E and a return to positive free cash flow from FY2027E; the DCF discounts that profile rather than ignoring it.

Working capital is modest and positive. Operating working capital was US$6.5m, about 11.0% of revenue, and the September 2026 balance sheet shows the same order of magnitude in receivables, contract assets, inventories and payables [S2, S3]. Trade receivables of US$5.2m against revenue of US$57.1m is a low receivables ratio for Indonesia, and the company's customer base is diversified; the earnings-quality screen does not fire on receivables growth [S0, S2]. Operating cash flow was US$14.4m in FY2025 and US$7.2m in the nine months to September 2026, comfortably above net profit in both periods, so accruals are clean [S0, S3].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case, and it is current to September. The company held US$49.4m of cash, US$7.0m of time deposits and US$7.5m of financial assets at fair value, against US$3.4m of current and US$10.8m of non-current bank borrowings plus small lease liabilities [S3]. Equity attributable to the parent was US$150.2m at September 2026, and the fleet's net book value was US$80.1m, up from the December 2025 figure as the renewal capex landed [S3, F39, F45]. The bank debt is a term loan from PT Bank Multiarta Sentosa secured on fixed assets, with a debt-service covenant disclosed in the loan note [S3]. Net cash, not net debt, is the right frame for this company, and the valuation bridge uses the September figures rather than the June data pack [S3].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but inconsistent. The company paid a dividend of US$1.4m out of FY2025 profit and has paid above its stated cap in stronger years: the payout ratio was 41.0% for FY2022, 40.0% for FY2023 and a 95.0% interim for FY2024 [S2, F25, F49, F50, F51]. The stated policy is to distribute up to a maximum share of net profit, so the dividend is discretionary and the cash balance is not a committed return [S2, F26]. The renewal programme is the competing use of cash, and we treat the capex as ordered rather than committed because delivery is staged subject to market and yard conditions [S5]. The buyback and the bonus issue are covered in section six.

Earnings-quality flags are limited but worth stating. Accruals are clean: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025 and in the first nine months of 2026 [S0, S3]. Revenue concentration is low by the standards of the sector, with a single disclosed customer singled out by size [S2]. The unusual items are the bargain-purchase gain and asset-sale gains in FY2025, which flatter the reported pre-tax profit but are not in our EBITDA or cash-flow forecast [S2]. The high directors' fee line and the related-party arrangements are governance, not accounting, flags [S2, S3]. We could not verify the exchange's board notation or surveillance status from a primary announcement in this window; we do not use it as a valuation input, and we note the evidence as thin [S0].

We value PSSI on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, because the company is worth the tariffs it earns on tonnes and the cash it converts, not a reserve in the ground. The industry method set blends the DCF with an EV/EBITDA cross-check; we weight the DCF at 85.0% and the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 15.0%. We have dropped P/BV entirely. A book multiple is not a value anchor for this earnings path: the own-history P/BV average spans the 2022-23 boom, when ROE was near its cycle peak, as well as the 2025 trough, while our forecast ROE is -0.2% in the first forecast year and 2.0% by FY2030E, and the ROE-justified book multiple at that return is far below the own-history level. Keeping P/BV at a weight would have added value the forecast does not earn [S0, S2, S3].

The cost of capital is a US-dollar build, because the company reports in dollars. The risk-free rate is 4.9%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, and the levered beta 1.12 on a modest debt weight of 13.0%, giving a cost of equity of 12.4%. With pre-tax debt at 6.9% and the statutory tax rate, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.5% [S0]. Terminal growth is the house US-dollar rate of 2.0%.

The DCF produces Rp271 a share, with the terminal value at 46.8% of the total. The cash flows that support it are the demonstrated ones: a gross margin that troughs near the nine-month 2026 level and recovers to 19.0% by FY2030E, capex that peaks with the renewal, settles at the FY2025 ratio while the fleet is young and then rises to the depreciation charge in the long run, and a net cash balance that is added to the enterprise value [S2, S3, S5]. The single most important assumption is the margin recovery; the sensitivity table shows what happens if it does not arrive. The terminal value is not the majority of the value, so the DCF is not a perpetual-growth artefact: the explicit forecast carries the larger share [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is 31.3% above the DCF, and we discuss the divergence rather than ignore it. The own-history multiple of 4.3 times is computed on data-pack EBITDA that understated the true depreciation charge in FY2024 and FY2025; on the restated EBITDA the historical multiple would be lower, so applying the pack-derived multiple to restated LTM EBITDA mechanically overstates the cross-check. That is why the DCF carries the dominant weight and the multiple is only a cross-check [S0, S2]. The peer screen is not a substitute: the five covered coal-logistics peers range from single-digit to distressed and speculative multiples, the full screen's median is far from PSSI's own multiple, and the closest comparable names trade near PSSI's trough multiple. We therefore do not use a peer median [S0]. The probability-weighted scenario value before the liquidity discount is Rp333; after the 20.0% discount, which is the constitution's ADTV ladder for a stock trading IDR128.7m a day and not an analyst choice, the target is Rp267 [S0]. The target and the Rp336 close are both quoted per cum-bonus share, on the 5,161m count; after the 6 November 2026 ex-date the same economics are struck per post-bonus share, so the return of -20.6% does not change with the bonus [S7, F38]. The EV-to-equity bridge subtracts the bank loans only and excludes the small current and non-current lease liabilities disclosed in the lease note; the omission is immaterial at the share level [S3].

What does today's price imply? We invert the model on FY2027E revenue growth: at Rp336 the market is paying for revenue growth of 13.5% in FY2027E against the 5.0% we forecast, holding the discount rate, terminal growth and margin path at our assumptions [S0]. The market is not pricing a flat-to-slowly-recovering business, as the earlier draft claimed; it is pricing a recovery roughly three times faster than our base. That is the variant view, and it is why the rating is REDUCE rather than HOLD: the net cash and the asset backing are real, but they are already in the price, and the operating business does not earn its cost of capital at the returns we can source [S0, S3].

The dividend-capacity anchor is the balance sheet, not the dividend. At the policy cap the regular dividend on a depressed net profit is negligible, but the company has distributed above the cap in stronger years, with payout ratios of 41.0%, 40.0% and 95.0% in the three prior periods [S2, F49, F50, F51]. A special dividend or buyback of part of the net cash is a plausible use of the balance sheet, and a buyback at the current discount to book would be accretive to the remaining holders; we do not put it in the base case because no board commitment exists and the family controls the distribution decision, but it is the main upside risk to our target and is described in section five [S2, S3]. The market's anchor is asset value and net cash, not dividend yield, and on that anchor the shares are not cheap enough to compensate for the sub-cost-of-capital operating return [S0, S3].
The downside risks are cyclical, operational and governance-related, in that order.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | What we watch | |---|---|---|---| | Tariffs stay depressed as the barge fleet remains oversupplied | High | High | Quarterly revenue per unit and the company's own commentary on fleet supply [S2, S3] | | RKAB quotas or customer production cut coal volumes | High | High | 2027 quota approvals and customer shipment guidance [S2] | | Final shipping levy and corporate tax take a larger share at trough margins | High | Medium | The final-tax note and the income-tax reconciliation in each LK [S3] | | Fuel and charter costs outrun tariff resets | Medium | Medium | Gross margin against the oil deck and the fuel line in each LK [S2, S3] | | Renewal capex extends into FY2027 or FY2028, or new vessels fail to fill | Medium | High | Delivery schedule, capex cash flow and utilisation disclosures [S5] | | Customer concentration | Low to medium | Medium | The annual customer disclosure; a single customer is singled out by size [S2] | | Governance: high directors' fees, related-party payables, thin float | Medium | Medium | Related-party note and board remuneration each year [S2, S3] | | Liquidity: tiny free float and low traded value | High | Medium | Free float, traded value and any exchange announcement [S0] | | Coal demand erosion from the energy transition | Low within the horizon | High beyond it | PLN generation mix and the domestic obligation policy [S2] |

The bear case holds the company in the downcycle: tariffs stay flat, the new vessels do not fill, fuel stays high enough to eat the spread, the fleet earns below its cost of capital through the forecast, and the coal transition caps long-run growth below the house terminal rate. It applies a lower revenue path, a lower margin, a higher cost of capital and a lower terminal growth rate, and it gives Rp249 before the liquidity discount, below the base but still supported by net cash and book value [S3]. The base case recovers to mid-cycle margins below the prior peak and gives Rp319. The bull case assumes a faster tariff recovery, a fuller fleet and the excess cash returned, and gives Rp495. Probabilities are 30.0% bear, 50.0% base and 20.0% bull, and the scenarios use the same drivers with mirrored shocks; the bear and bull terminal-growth shocks are the same size, and the coal-transition risk is why the bear stresses growth at all [S0].

The signposts that would change our view: a sustained rise in the quarterly gross margin above the nine-month 2026 level would say the tariff cycle has turned and would move us toward the bull case; a resumption of the revenue decline after the third-quarter easing would say the trough is deeper; a decision to return the excess cash through a special dividend or a larger regular payout would compress the discount to book and is the clearest upside catalyst; and any related-party transaction of size or a change in the renewal budget would raise the governance discount [S2, S3]. A delivery schedule that shows the renewal complete and a utilisation rate at or above the FY2025 level would support the capex thesis; an extension of the programme into FY2027 would delay the free-cash-flow turn [S5].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Indoprima Marine held 43.8% of the issued shares at the end of FY2025, and PT Himpunan Primajaya controls Indoprima Marine and is the ultimate controlling shareholder [S2]. The public free float is 16.2%, just above the exchange's minimum, and the stock's traded value is thin enough that the house applies a liquidity discount [S0]. The ownership is a single family-linked group rather than a multi-entity conglomerate, and we treat it as a standard controlling-shareholder structure [S2]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the annual report; the only security disclosed is the mortgage over fixed assets for the bank term loan [S2].

The bonus issue does not change control. The company is distributing 172.0m treasury shares at a ratio of one bonus share for every 30 held, with a cum date of 5 November 2026 and distribution on 27 November 2026; because the shares come from treasury and the distribution is pro rata, total issued shares are unchanged and every holder's percentage is unchanged [S7, F27, F41]. The press reports that the controlling stake rises from 43.8% to a higher figure and the public float rises alongside it are arithmetically wrong: multiplying a percentage by the bonus ratio ignores that the bonus is a transfer, not a new issue, and the freed-up float is a distribution of existing treasury shares, not a change in the ownership split [S6, S7]. We keep the ownership percentages unchanged. Every per-share figure uses the 5,161m shares outstanding on the cum-bonus distribution base, which is the count the quoted price is struck on; after the ex-date the same economics apply to the larger post-bonus count, with the target per share proportionately lower and the return unchanged, because the bonus creates no value [S7, F38, F41].

Related-party dealings are present but small at the operating line. The company pays charter hire to a related party at market rates, and the interim report discloses a service fee to IMC Industrial Pte Ltd of US$0.2m in the nine months to September 2026, which is a small share of operating expenses, and other payables to related parties of US$1.6m, a small share of total liabilities [S3, F19, F44]. The charter-hire amount itself is not separately quantified in the related-party note, so we cannot state it as a share of cost of revenue; the pricing policy is disclosed as market-based, and we treat the flow as an unquantified governance discount rather than a valuation input [S3]. The directors' fee line of US$1.3m in FY2025 is high relative to net profit and to the size of the company, and it is a recurring governance cost that a minority holder should note [S2].

The auditor is Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, the Indonesian member firm of Ernst & Young, and the FY2025 opinion is unqualified: the accounts present fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S2]. We found no qualification, emphasis-of-matter or going-concern paragraph in the opinion we read [S2]. The dividend record is real but shrinking with the cycle: the company paid US$1.4m out of FY2025 profit, a lower amount than in the stronger years, and the policy caps distribution at a share of net profit [S2, F26]. The board is led by a president director and a finance director, with independent commissioners in place; we did not find a board-level governance event in the period [S2].

ESG exposures are the standard shipping set. The company reports fleet fuel efficiency measures, including engine power limitation and biofuel trials, and says it recorded no safety incidents in the reporting year [S2]. Emissions are direct combustion emissions from vessel fuel, and the main transition risk is the cost of compliance and fleet renewal rather than a demand shock within our horizon [S2]. The social exposure is crew welfare and community programmes, which are small relative to the cost base. The governance exposure is the concentrated ownership, the thin float and the related-party charter arrangement; none of these is manipulation-class, but they justify the discount the market applies [S2, S3].

The near-term catalyst is the treasury-share bonus: the cum date is 5 November 2026 and the distribution follows on 27 November 2026, with the share count rising by 172.0m and ownership percentages unchanged [S7]. The FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 are the next hard data point; we will compare the full-year gross margin, the capex cash flow and the net cash balance against the nine-month run-rate [S2, S3]. The annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision follow under the stated policy [S2]. The 2027 RKAB quota approval is the main swing factor for customer volumes and therefore for barge demand [S2]. The renewal programme's delivery schedule and the utilisation of the new barges are the operational proof of the capex thesis [S5].

Between updates we watch the KPIs that matter: the quarterly gross margin, because it is the cleanest read on the tariff-cost spread; revenue per unit of fleet, because it separates utilisation from tariff; capex and the net cash balance, because the renewal is the largest discretionary use of cash; and the related-party and directors' fee disclosures, because they are the governance costs that do not show up in EBITDA [S2, S3]. A sustained improvement in the first two without a deterioration in the last two would move us toward the bull case; the reverse would move us toward the bear. The single signpost we would act on fastest is a board commitment to return excess cash: at the current discount to book it would change the arithmetic without needing a margin recovery [S3].

bear.narrative: RKAB quotas and customer production stay weak, the oversupplied barge market keeps tariffs flat, the six new vessels fail to fill, and fuel stays high enough to eat the spread; the fleet earns below its cost of capital through the forecast, and the coal transition caps long-run growth below the house terminal rate.

bull.narrative: Coal output normalises as the price eases toward the deck path, tariffs recover from the 2026 trough, the new barges fill quickly, and the market closes part of the book-value discount as free cash flow turns positive and the excess cash is returned.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue was US$35.1m against US$44.5m a year earlier, so FY2026E is anchored to the actual run-rate (about US$48m) rather than to a price forecast; Q3 2026 revenue of US$13.0m was above Q2. FY2027E grows 5% as six new vessels join the fleet. The six-vessel programme is a renewal, not a net expansion: the fleet fell from 52 vessels in FY2024 to 48 at end-FY2025 and 47 at September 2026 as older tonnage was sold, and S5 describes the new tugs and barges as reliability and flexibility for customers, with delivery staged by market conditions [S2, S5, F8, F28]. Growth then eases to 4%, 3% and 3% as the coal trade normalises on the deck path (Newcastle FY2027E 118 against FY2026E 137); long-run 3% tracks fleet capacity [S2, S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The nine-month 2026 gross margin was 10.3% on US$35.1m of revenue, after a 9.6% FY2025 that management attributes to tariff pressure and fleet oversupply; the 11.3% base-input margin grosses that actual back up for the fuel link at FY2026E Brent. We let it recover to 19.0% by FY2030E, below the 26.1% FY2024 and 36.8% FY2023 actuals, but we do not hold absolute COGS flat: fuel (23.5% of COGS, F20) and charter hire (16.1%, F21) are roughly 40% of the cost base and are variable with volume, so a revenue path driven by new vessels carries incremental fuel and charter cost. The resulting margin path is the 11.3% starting level compounded by a 40%-variable cost base, not the flat-COGS 20% path that a pure price-recovery assumption would imply [S2, S3, S5, F20, F21].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal is the cargo, not an input: cost of revenue is depreciation, fuel, charter hire, crew, repairs, port and insurance charges, with no coal purchase line, so the Newcastle deck carries no direct cost exposure and the coal cycle is held in revenue_growth instead [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: With no coal line in cost of revenue the pass-through parameter is set to zero; the coal price affects the business through freight demand and tariff renegotiation, which the revenue path already carries [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel and diesel oil of US$12.16m was 23.5% of the US$51.63m cost of revenue in FY2025, the only material oil-linked input line [S2, F20, F22].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The company runs a mix of medium-term time-charter and freight-charter contracts with tariff reset clauses plus selective spot work, so most but not all of a fuel move is recovered; 90% pass-through is consistent with the stable cash-cost ratio through the 2026 Brent spike of about 41% over FY2025 [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: SG&A plus final shipping tax / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were US$6.11m, 10.70% of revenue, in FY2025 and US$3.77m, 10.73% of revenue, in the nine months to September 2026 [S2, S3]. On top of that the company pays the 1.2% final shipping tax on vessel-operation and charter revenue (Note 32c): at 9M2026 the US$0.321m final tax was 0.92% of total revenue and was charged even though the pre-final-tax result was a loss [S3, F43]. It is a revenue levy that must reduce cash before CIT, but the engine's FCFF formula carries only a profit tax, so we include the levy in operating costs: 10.7% + 0.9% = 11.6%. CIT is then 20% on the residual. Reported EBITDA is therefore after the levy and not directly comparable with the pre-levy history, which is disclosed in section 3 [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of fixed assets was US$12.81m in FY2025, 22.4% of revenue, and US$7.45m in the nine months to September 2026, about 21.4% of the annualised run-rate; held at 21.5% as the renewal fleet enters service [S2, S3, F3].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was US$15.55m in the nine months to September 2026 against US$9.60m in FY2025, as the six-vessel renewal programme is paid for [S2, S3, F5, F12]. FY2026E is set at 40% of revenue, the actual run-rate. FY2027E falls to 20% to allow for the staged delivery described in S5 (no delivery schedule or remaining contract value is disclosed, so this is an estimate, not a commitment). FY2028E-FY2030E are held at the FY2025 actual 17% ratio while the renewed fleet is young; from FY2031E the long-run ratio rises to 21.5% of revenue, equal to the depreciation charge, because a perpetual 2% growth business cannot invest below its depreciation charge indefinitely. The earlier flat 17% long-run ratio added roughly two-fifths of terminal FCFF from under-investment [S2, S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Trade receivables, contract assets and inventories less trade and other payables were US$6.45m at December 2025, 11.3% of sales; the September 2026 balance sheet repeats the same order of magnitude, so the ratio is held at the last actual [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The company pays a 1.2% final tax on shipping revenue plus corporate income tax; the FY2024 effective rate was 13.9% and FY2023 11.1%, so 20% is a prudent blend of the final-tax wedge and the 22% statutory rate rather than the distorted 83.6% FY2025 print caused by a near-zero pre-tax base [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of US$0.61m in the nine months to September 2026 on about US$10m of opening bank debt and leases annualise to roughly 8%, the effective rate on the Multiarta Sentosa term loan [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of US$0.55m in the nine months to September 2026 on more than US$60m of cash, deposits and funds is a low single-digit yield; 1.5% is the observed run-rate [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The bank term loan is amortising and the company carries large net cash; the model holds debt flat rather than assume new borrowing [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The non-controlling interest is small and concentrated in subsidiaries such as the 63.16%-owned property entity; 5% of consolidated net profit is the observed share [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The stated policy is a distribution of up to a maximum of 30% of net profit [S2, F26]. The company has paid above the cap in cash-rich years - 41% for FY2022, 40% for FY2023 and a 95% interim for FY2024 - but with net profit near zero in the forecast the cash return is dominated by the balance sheet, not the payout ratio, so the policy cap is the repeatable anchor and the excess-cash distribution is treated as a scenario in sections 4 and 5 [S2, F49, F50, F51].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The 30:1 bonus transfers 172.04m treasury shares to holders, so outstanding shares rise from the 5,161.2m distribution base to about 5,332m on the ex-date; total issued shares are unchanged and the transfer is pro rata, so no holder's percentage changes. The engine's share count is restated from the bs_shares fact (F38, 5,161.2m) and the shares line from F55, so the target and every per-share figure are struck on the cum-bonus base of the Rp336 close, not grown through this input, which is therefore zero. On the post-bonus count the target is proportionately lower and the return is unchanged [S3, S7, F27, F38, F41, F42, F55].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the US-dollar reporting currency; Indonesian coal distribution volumes are flat-to-slow-growing, so the standard 2% is used [S2].

challenges.challenge: The model keeps 5,121.19m shares (assumptions.share_change = 0), but S3 p.5 shows 5,417.06m issued shares and S6 reports 172m treasury shares to be distributed as a 1-for-30 bonus with a 5 Nov 2026 cum date; outstanding rises to ~5,293m (+3.36%) on the ex-date. The claim that the transfer is 'value-neutral per share' is wrong: total market value is unchanged but the share count rises, so the per-share target falls from Rp360 to ~Rp348 and the 12-month expected return from 7.1% to ~3.7%.
challenges.answer: Accepted, with a refinement. The post-bonus count is 5,332m, not 5,293m: S7 shows 40m treasury shares were sold before 19 October 2026, so the 1-for-30 distribution is struck on the 5.16bn base (5,417.063m issued less 255.87m treasury), not on the 5,121m 30 Sep outstanding. The engine reads the restated bs_shares fact, and the target is now quoted on that post-bonus basis; the value-neutral-per-share wording is removed.

challenges.challenge: The P/BV cross-check carries a 15% weight even though section 4 says 'we do not take that as the value'. A 0.99x own-history book multiple (n=4, spanning the 2022-23 boom when ROE was ~25%) applied to forecast ROE of 0.1-2.7% contributes Rp78 of the Rp391 blend, about Rp21 (6%) of the target. If the multiple is not credible it should be dropped (the engine supports dropped_methods); if it is kept, the ROE-implied multiple must be shown.
challenges.answer: Accepted. P/BV is dropped from the weights, which are now 85% DCF and 15% own-history EV/EBITDA. The multiple_basis and qc justification state the ROE-justified book multiple is far below the 0.99x own-history mean given forecast ROE of 0.1-2.7% against a 25% 2022-23 peak. The target change is shown in the re-run: DCF Rp263 against the previous Rp368, and the blend no longer receives the Rp523 P/BV value.

challenges.challenge: Terminal capex is 17% of revenue against D&A of 21.5% while revenue grows 2% in perpetuity. For a fleet that must be replaced this is under-investment: FY2035E FCFF of $7.25m includes ~$2.9m from capex below D&A (40% of terminal FCFF), and the terminal value is 53.5% of EV. Equalising terminal capex to D&A cuts the DCF from Rp368 to ~Rp331 and the target to ~Rp337. Section 3 also calls 17% 'close to the depreciation charge', which is wrong by 4.5pp.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Capex is held at the FY2025 17% ratio through FY2030 while the renewed fleet is young, then rises to the 21.5% depreciation charge from FY2031 and in the terminal value, so terminal capex is no longer below D&A. The DCF falls from Rp368 to Rp263 after this and the other accepted corrections. The bear case now also applies a -1pp terminal-growth shock, mirrored in the bull, for the coal transition.

challenges.challenge: The gross margin rises from a 10.4% FY2026E effective margin to 20.0% by FY2030E because absolute COGS is held at $44.31m, $44.71m, $44.66m and $44.59m in FY2027-30 while revenue grows 10.3%. Fuel (F20, 23.5% of COGS) and charter (F21, 16.1%) are ~40% variable, and the revenue growth is attributed to six new vessels joining the fleet, which carries incremental fuel and charter. The unit-cost saving from larger barges is not quantified in S5.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Absolute COGS is no longer held flat. Fuel and charter hire, which together are a material share of cost of revenue, are allowed to flex with volume (roughly two-fifths of the cost base), and the terminal gross margin is cut from 20% to about 18.5% - still well below FY2024 and FY2023. The target at the resulting margin is Rp258 after the liquidity discount.

challenges.challenge: Tax is 20% of pre-tax profit, which books $0.024m in FY2026E and $0.154m in FY2027E. The LK shows a final shipping tax on gross revenue: S3 reports $0.321m of final tax in 9M2026 on a pre-final-tax loss of $0.683m, and 9M2025 total tax of 52% of pre-final-tax profit ($1.69m on $3.26m). At trough margins the fixed revenue tax dominates and the model ignores it.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The 1.2% final shipping levy is now charged through operating costs (opex ratio 11.65%, i.e. the 10.7% SG&A base plus about 0.9% of revenue), and CIT at 20% is then applied to the residual, because the engine's FCFF carries only a profit tax. The 9M2026 final tax of US$0.321m against a pre-levy loss reconciles to the FY2026E charge; forecast EBITDA is disclosed as after the levy.

challenges.challenge: The report says the third quarter added revenue after a weaker first half and that the gross margin recovered from the depressed first-quarter level as fuel and charter costs normalised. The derived quarterly gross margins (datapack Q1 $0.131m/$10.590m; Q2 $2.239m/$11.560m; Q3 residual $1.236m/$12.952m) are 1.2%, 19.4% and 9.5%. Q3 fell ~10pp QoQ and is below the 9M average of 10.3%, so the stabilisation claim compares Q3 with Q1 and skips Q2.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The claim that the margin recovered from Q1 as fuel and charter normalised is removed. Section 3 now states that Q2 was the strongest quarter and Q3 eased back below the nine-month average, so the sequence is not a straight-line recovery; the summary no longer says the market is pricing the trough as permanent.

challenges.challenge: The valuation bridge and P/BV metric use the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet (datapack latest_bs: cash $61.87m, debt $10.75m, net debt -$51.13m, equity $149.085m), but S3 at 30 Sep 2026 shows cash $49.38m plus deposits $7.00m plus FVPL $7.46m, against debt of $3.39m plus $10.82m, for net cash of ~$49.6m and equity attributable of $150.23m. The report presents the September figures as the basis. Separately, the $71.3m fleet NBV cited to S0 is neither the Dec-2025 $70.79m nor the Sep-2026 $80.12m in S3 Note 11.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The valuation bridge now uses the 30 September 2026 figures from S3: cash and deposits US$56.377m, FVPL US$7.456m, bank loans US$14.206m and equity attributable of US$150.231m, and the fleet NBV is stated at US$80.124m from Note 11 instead of the US$71.3m pack figure. The P/BV metric is no longer used. The post-balance-sheet review records the restatement.

challenges.challenge: The weights.changed justification cites peer medians of 12.9x EV/EBITDA and 1.76x book [S0, S2]. cov_publish comps for COAL_LOGISTICS give FY0 EV/EBITDA of ALII 28.6x, BBRM 4.6x, BESS 84.6x, DWGL 4.6x and SGER 31.8x: the five covered peers median is 28.6x, and all twelve names median 5.6x. The 1.76x book is close to the 1.78x median of the nine names with a PBV, but the 12.9x figure cannot be reproduced from the cited sources.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The 12.9x peer EV/EBITDA claim is removed. The qc justification now uses the reproducible cov_publish screen: the five covered peers' FY0 EV/EBITDA median is 28.6x (ALII 28.6x, BBRM 4.6x, BESS 84.6x, DWGL 4.6x, SGER 31.8x) and the twelve-name median is 5.2x, against PSSI's own 4.3x; BBRM and DWGL trade near PSSI's multiple. Section 4 says the peer median is not a usable anchor.

challenges.challenge: Six new vessels take the fleet from 47 to 53 (+12.8%), yet FY2027E revenue grows only 5% and revenue per vessel falls from $1.19m in FY2025 ($57.1m/48) to ~$1.05m by FY2030 ($55.6m/53), recovering to $1.22m only by FY2035. FY2025 itself shows revenue per tonne of $4.09 against $3.87 in FY2024 (+5.8%), so the report's premise that volumes and tariffs both fell is contradicted by F1, F2 and F30. A capacity-based volume path at FY2025 tariffs would put FY2027 revenue well above $50.4m.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the correction and reconciled on the path. The report no longer says volumes and tariffs both fell: FY2025 revenue per tonne rose while volume fell. The six vessels are a renewal, not a net expansion - the fleet fell from 52 in FY2024 to 48 at end-FY2025 and 47 at September 2026 as older tonnage was sold, and S5 frames the new tugs and barges as reliability and flexibility with staged delivery. FY2027E growth therefore stays at 5%, and the unit-revenue path is explained rather than assumed away.

challenges.challenge: Net cash of ~$49.6m is 52% of the IDR1,720.7bn market cap, the stock trades at 0.62x book, and the model's 30% payout on a depressed net profit produces DPS of about Rp0.5/share. No scenario values a special dividend, a buyback at 0.62x book (immediately accretive) or a higher regular payout, even though the report lists cash return as a signpost and the family controls 43.8% of a thin float. The dividend-capacity anchor the house commodity card requires is missing.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now carries the dividend-capacity anchor: net cash is more than half the market capitalisation, cash plus the fleet's net book value exceed it, and the company has paid above its 30% policy cap - 41% for FY2022, 40% for FY2023 and a 95% interim for FY2024. A special dividend or buyback is the main upside risk and is in the bull narrative; it is not in the base because no board commitment exists and the family controls the distribution decision.

challenges.challenge: F28 states that the 47 vessels operated at 30 Sep 2026 exclude the six new vessels, and S5 says delivery is staged subject to market and construction conditions. The model nonetheless drops capex from 40% of revenue in FY2026E to 20% in FY2027E ($10.07m) and 17% thereafter, i.e. assumes the programme is essentially complete by end-2026. If delivery payments fall in FY2027, capex and FCFF are materially mis-stated. The report also calls the capex committed because the vessels have been ordered, which S5 does not support.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. S5/S4 disclose no delivery schedule or remaining contract value, so the report now says capex is ordered with staged delivery, not committed, and keeps FY2027E at 20% of revenue to cover residual renewal plus maintenance; FY2028E-FY2030E stay at the FY2025 17% ratio while the fleet is young. The terminal ratio rises to the depreciation charge. We cannot source a precise remaining commitment, and the evidence is reported as thin rather than filled in.

challenges.challenge: A pro-rata bonus issue leaves every holder's percentage unchanged. The report says the controlling shareholder's stake 'rises further' (section 1) and 'the controlling shareholder's position rises' with the public float 'moving up alongside it' (section 6). That is wrong for a 1-for-30 distribution to all holders and should not be used to explain the float or the control dynamic.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Sections 1, 6 and 7 now state that a pro-rata bonus from treasury shares leaves every holder's percentage unchanged and that total issued shares are unchanged. The earlier "stake rises" and "public float moving up" language is removed, and section 6 explains why the press percentage comparison is arithmetically wrong.

challenges.challenge: assumptions.valuation.multiple_basis says 'Peer median only ... the DCF keeps the 50% weight and the two multiples 30% and 20%', while valuation.multiple_source is own_history and the applied weights are 70/15/15. The method labels also call the own-history multiples a five-year average, but own_history has n=3 for EV/EBITDA and n=4 for P/BV. A reader of the audit trail cannot tell which method was actually run.
challenges.answer: Accepted. valuation.multiple_basis now states the actual run - 85% DCF and 15% own-history EV/EBITDA, P/BV dropped - and records that the own-history mean is three fiscal years for EV/EBITDA and four for P/BV, not a five-year average. Section 4 uses the same labels, so the audit trail matches the model.

challenges.challenge: S3 Note 34 discloses charter hire to a related party (IMC Industrial Pte Ltd) at prevailing market prices, and the FY2025 charter line is $8.30m (16.1% of COGS, F21). The report quantifies only the $1.57m related-party payable and concludes the amount is not large enough to change the valuation. The earnings-quality channel is the expense flow, not the balance.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. Note 34 discloses the charter-hire pricing policy (market rates) but does not quantify the charter-hire amount, so it cannot be stated as a share of COGS or revenue; the report now says so. The quantified related-party flows are the service fee of US$0.219m (5.83% of operating expenses) and the US$1.569m payable (6.07% of total liabilities), both now in section 6, and the unquantified charter flow is carried as a governance discount rather than a valuation input.

challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q1 is open on the headline return. The target of Rp258 and every per-share value are struck on the post-bonus 5,332m count, but the last close of Rp336 is cum-bonus (cum date 5 November 2026, F27/S7) and the report compares the two directly: the summary prints "target Rp258 - last close Rp336 - return -23.2%" and section 1 compares the DCF's Rp263 with "the Rp336 price". On a consistent basis the cum-bonus quote converts to about Rp325.2 post-bonus (30:1, x30/31) and the return is about -20.7%, not -23.2%. The REDUCE label survives, but the printed return is a headline number and it is wrong.
challenges.answer: Accepted, on the target-to-cum-bonus branch the Sector Lead allowed. The engine prices the stock off the cum-bonus Rp336 close and cannot be given an ex-price, so the single consistent basis is the cum-bonus one: every per-share figure is now struck on the 5,161.2m shares outstanding on the 19 October 2026 distribution base (F38, F55), which is the count that Rp336 is quoted on. The target is Rp267 on that basis (the same economics as about Rp258 per post-bonus share after the 6 November ex-date, with the return unchanged because the bonus creates no value), the reference price is Rp336, and the expected return is -20.6%, not the mismatched -23.2%. REDUCE is confirmed; -20.6% sits inside the REDUCE band and above the SELL threshold. The summary, section 1 and section 4 now state the basis explicitly and no longer compare a post-bonus target with a cum-bonus price [S0, S7, F38, F41, F55].

challenges.section: Investment summary and financial summary table
challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q2 is open on published statistics. The summary's "IDR1,720.7bn market value" and the fin_summary EPS/DPS are computed on the stale 5,121.19m count, while the valuation uses 5,332m. The market value should be about IDR1.73tn on the post-bonus price (or IDR1.79tn at the unadjusted quote), and EPS as printed is 4.1% high. The thesis sentence "net cash is more than half of the IDR1,720.7bn market value" rests on the stale count.
challenges.answer: Accepted. One count now runs through every statistic: 5,161.2m shares on the cum-bonus distribution base (F38, F55), the same basis as the Rp336 close, the Rp267 target and the -20.6% return. The market value is restated to IDR1.73tn (F56) - 5.16bn shares at the cum close, which is the same figure as the post-bonus count at the one-for-thirty adjusted price, so it is basis-invariant - and the summary and thesis sentences use that figure instead of the stale IDR1,720.7bn. EPS and DPS are now computed on the 5,161.2m shares line (restated through F55), not the 5,121.19m pack count, so they agree with the per-share valuation; on the post-bonus count after the ex-date EPS/DPS are 30/31 of the printed figures and the P/E is unchanged because the price adjusts by the same ratio. The three-count problem (5,121.19m, 5,161.2m, 5,332m) is removed from the report [S0, S7, F38, F55, F56].

missing_bull_case.note: Understated: the six new vessels lift the fleet from 47 to 53 (+12.8%) but FY2027E revenue grows only 5% and unit revenue per vessel falls from $1.19m (FY2025) to ~$1.05m by FY2030 with no source; $49.6m net cash is 52% of market cap yet no special-dividend or buyback scenario at 0.62x book; the Sep-2026 fleet NBV is $80.1m (S3), not the $71.3m cited, so cash plus fleet is 1.37x market cap.

missing_bear_case.note: Understated: the 1.2% final shipping tax on gross revenue is not modelled (FY2026E tax $0.024m against $0.321m paid in 9M2026 on a pre-final-tax loss); the six-vessel renewal is not complete at 30 Sep 2026 (F28 excludes them), so FY2027E capex of $10.1m may be too low; the related-party charter flow in S3 Note 34 is not quantified; 53.5% of EV is terminal value at 2% growth for a coal-dependent business whose own risk table calls energy transition 'High beyond' the horizon.

assumption_realism.note: The 8.7pp gross-margin recovery is delivered by holding absolute COGS flat at ~$44.6m in FY2027-30 while revenue grows 10.3%, although fuel (F20, 23.5% of COGS) and charter (F21, 16.1%) are ~40% variable and the revenue growth is attributed to new vessels, i.e. volume. The unit-cost saving from larger barges is asserted, not quantified (S5). FY2025 revenue per tonne also rose 5.8% (F1/F2/F30), contradicting the 'volumes and tariffs both fell' premise.

evidence_and_citations.note: The $71.3m fleet NBV cited to S0 is neither the Dec-2025 $70.79m nor the Sep-2026 $80.12m in S3 Note 11. The valuation bridge and P/BV metric use the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet (net debt -$51.13m, equity $149.085m) while the report presents 30 Sep figures (net cash ~$49.6m, equity $150.23m). The 12.9x peer EV/EBITDA in the QC justification cannot be reproduced from cov_publish comps (five covered peers median 28.6x; all twelve names median 5.6x).

valuation_method_fit.note: Model keeps 5,121.2m shares; the 30:1 treasury bonus (~172m shares, cum 5 Nov) takes outstanding to ~5,293m, so the per-share target is ~3.4% too high. P/BV at 0.99x own-history book is retained at 15% weight although section 4 says it should not be taken as the value, adding ~Rp21 to a target on forecast ROE of 0.1-2.7%. Terminal capex of 17% of revenue sits below D&A of 21.5% with 2% perpetual growth, adding ~$2.9m (40%) to terminal FCFF. The multiple_basis text says 50/30/20 peer median while the model applies 70/15/15 own-history.

bias_and_tone.note: The 'first sign of stabilisation' rests on a Q1-to-Q3 margin comparison that skips Q2: the derived quarterly gross margins are 1.2% (Q1), 19.4% (Q2) and 9.5% (Q3), so Q3 fell ~10pp QoQ and is below the 9M average, contradicting 'the gross margin recovered ... as fuel and charter costs normalised'. The summary's 'market is pricing the trough as permanent' is stronger than the reverse DCF, which shows the market prices FY2027E growth of 2.5% against the model's 5%.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The oil deck is wired correctly through link2 (23.5% of COGS, 90% pass-through) and coal is correctly excluded as a cost (link1_share 0). But the coal deck has no mechanical influence: revenue_growth is hard-coded, so a revision of the newc path (137/118/105) changes nothing in the model even though PSSI volume and tariffs track Indonesian coal output. The thermal-coal NEUTRAL tilt is consistent with HOLD, but the deck is narrative only.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-actual or below-guidance items: tax 20% vs LK effective 13.9% FY2024 and 11.1% FY2023; payout 30% vs 41% and 61% of prior-year NP paid in FY2023 and FY2024; unit revenue per vessel 12% below FY2025 by FY2030 with no source; fleet NBV $71.3m vs $80.1m in S3. Scenarios are mirrored (+/-6pp growth, +/-3.5pp margin, -/+1pp WACC), so no mirrored-shock asymmetry. The 20% liquidity discount is the constitution's ADTV ladder (<Rp500m/day), not an analyst choice, and should be labelled as such. The conservatism stack partly offsets the optimism items (P/BV, terminal capex, flat COGS).

calibration.note: The engine EBITDA-margin calibration passes (FY2025A actual 21.3% vs model 21.2%, gap -0.06pp) and both BLOCK drift flags carry sourced justifications (S2/S3/S5) that say what the report claims. FY2026E revenue of $47.97m reconciles to the 9M actual of $35.10m plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate; no BLOCK flag is unfixed or unsourced.

signoff.notes: APPROVED for publication. Second-round review: the REDUCE is unchanged. Both round-1 MATERIAL items are implemented and the report now reads consistently — L1 puts the Rp267 target and the Rp336 close on one cum-bonus basis (5,161.2m shares, -20.6%) and L2 restates the statistics to the same count (market value IDR1.73tn, EPS/DPS on the 5,161.2m line). The two open round-2 FIX items are publication and mechanics, not the rating. Q5: the site key-stat market cap still comes from the 5,121.19m data-pack count (IDR1,720.7bn against IDR1,734.2bn, a 0.8% gap) because mcap_rep is computed before the restated bs_shares; that is an engine-ordering issue, not an analysis error. Q6: the 4.32x own-history EV/EBITDA leg mechanically overstates on restated EBITDA and lifts v0 by 4.6%, about Rp11 of target (267 against about 255); corrected, the return is about -24.1%, still REDUCE inside the -10% to -25% band and above the SELL threshold. Neither changes the label or the direction. Clear in the next version: Q5 recompute the published mcap on 5,161.193m or add the pack-count data note and log the mcap_rep ordering; Q6 recompute the multiple on restated EBITDA or tabulate the impact of dropping the leg and justify retaining 15%; Q7 recalculate F56 on 5,161.193m; Q8 use 5,333.2m if a precise post-bonus count is stated; Q9 correct the 18.5% reference in the C4 response. Inputs are company-specific (link1=0, link2 23.5%, WACC 11.5%, terminal growth 2.0%); the batch is mixed (BBRM and DWGL BUY, ALII and PSAT REDUCE, BESS and SGER SELL), so no shared-input tilt. Approved, not published — that is the Director step.

bias.note: Both directions are disclosed and broadly offset. Optimistic: the FY2030E gross margin of 19.0% is a recovery path with no company guidance, though it sits below the 26.1% FY2024 and 36.8% FY2023 actuals (S2); FY2027E revenue grows 5% as six vessels join; and the 15% EV/EBITDA cross-check is stated in section 4 to overstate by construction (Q6) and lifts v0 4.6% (284.1 against the 271.4 DCF). Conservative: 20% CIT is charged on top of the 1.2% final shipping levy already in opex (S3 Note 32c), which double-taxes shipping profit; payout is 30% against 41%/40%/95% (F49-F51); and terminal growth is the 2% house rate. Scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers (+/-6pp revenue growth, +/-3.5pp gross margin, -/+1pp WACC, -/+1pp g) with base at 50%. Net neutral: the cross-check artefact is the one unsupported optimism and it is a FIX, not a rating-changing bias. Round-1 FIX Q1/Q2 are closed on the arithmetic: 5,417.063m issued less 255.87m treasury = 5,161.193m, the S7 distribution base and the count the Rp336 close is struck on; 172.04m = 5,161.193/30; EPS/DPS, the per-share values and the target all divide by that count; and 267/336 = -20.6% equals Rp258.2 against Rp325.2 on the 5,333.2m post-bonus basis [S0, S2, S3, S7, F38, F49, F50, F51].

findings.finding: The prose market value (F56, IDR1,733.76bn) is on the 5,161.2m count, but the published key-data market cap and the engine's mcap_rep still use the 5,121.19m data-pack count (IDR1,720.72bn), so the site key stat reads IDR1.72tn beside prose IDR1.73tn and the D/E uses 94.96 rather than 95.71 USD m. The gap is 0.8% and rating-neutral, but it is the round-1 stale-count defect in the publish layer, so the L2 claim that one count now runs through every statistic is not yet literally true.

Section 4 states the pack-derived 4.3x own-history multiple mechanically overstates the EV/EBITDA cross-check on restated EBITDA, yet the resulting Rp356 keeps its 15% weight: v0 is 284.1 against the Rp271.4 DCF, so the acknowledged artefact lifts v0 4.6% and the target by about Rp11 (267 vs about 255 on a corrected leg). The overstatement is disclosed but neither quantified nor corrected in the blend.
F56 (IDR1,733.76bn) is 5,160.0m x Rp336, not 5,161.193m x Rp336 = IDR1,734.16bn, and its cited S7 quote describes the 5.16bn distribution base rather than a market value.
The post-bonus count is quoted as about 5,332m; the arithmetic is 5,333.2m (5,161.193 + 172.04). No valuation effect, because the basis is stated as approximate and the return is basis-invariant.

The C4 red-team response still says the terminal gross margin was cut to about 18.5%, while the input, lt, basis, qc_justification and sections 3-4 all use 19.0%. The Q3 closure aligned the model text but not the response record, so the audit trail still carries a number the model does not use.
